rows.title: Online Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Videos with Asymptotic Bound on False Alarm Rate (MONAD); arXiv title uses 'Bounds'
rows.venue_year: Pattern Recognition 114 (June 2021) 107865, DOI 10.1016/j.patcog.2021.107865 (confirmed on Crossref); arXiv 2010.07110v1, Oct 2020
rows.causality_evidence: PAPER (arXiv v1, Sec. 3.6, 4.5): the frame predictor uses the previous 4 frames. The CUSUM statistic s_t = max(s_{t-1}+delta_t, 0) is causal. But after s_t crosses h, frames from tau_start (last time s_t was 0) up to the alarm are relabelled anomalous, which is a retroactive relabel. tau_end needs about 5 later frames of decreasing statistic. Sec. 4.5 says only that the ShanghaiTech result is 'based on online decision making without seeing future video frames'. It makes no such statement for Ped2 or Avenue. CODE (the official repo MONAD.ipynb, Ped2 only) refutes an online evaluation for Ped2: (1) the per-video baseline is lm2=[0.75,...,0.95,0.85,...]; a comment says it is computed per video from that test video's mean and variance. (2) After each video is scored, positive frames are pruned using the indices of later positive frames in the same video, which is look-ahead. (3) The final score is min-max normalised per video: (vid-min)/(max-min). Scores are then concatenated for sklearn roc_curve. (4) A hand-added ROC point (fpr 0.45, tpr 1) is appended, and fpr and tpr are sorted separately. The printed result is 'ODIT AUC: 0.977', not the 97.2 in the paper.
rows.shtech_auc: 70.9 (107 test videos, 13 scenes per paper text)
rows.auc_table_ref: arXiv 2010.07110v1 Table 1 (frame-level AuROC on concatenated videos). Fig. 4: low-FPR ROC against an 'online' Liu et al. (training-set min/max) on Ped2 and ShT. Published PR version not accessible (403), so I did not check whether its numbers differ.
rows.fps_or_latency: GAN frame predictor 22 fps; YOLOv3 about 12 ms per frame (about 83 fps) on an RTX 2070 with an i7-8700K. No end-to-end fps is stated; it is bounded by the 22 fps predictor.
rows.code_url: https://github.com/kevaldoshi17/Prediction-based-Video-Anomaly-Detection- (Ped2 notebook only; no Avenue or ShT evaluation code)
rows.notes: Correction to the searcher: the paper does not say 'only' ShT is online. It singles out ShT, and the code shows Ped2 is evaluated with per-video normalisation, which is exactly what the paper criticises in Liu 2018. The notebook also restricts test-time YOLO classes to person/skateboard/bicycle/skis, which includes the Ped2 anomaly classes. It uses different detector confidence thresholds for train (0.97) and test (0.6). The same feature pipeline and identical numbers appear in ODIT (Sensors 2022). The online decision rule itself is real, but the reported frame-AUC must not be treated as a causal-evaluation number.

rows.title: Any-Shot Sequential Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Videos
rows.venue_year: CVPR 2020 Workshops (CLVision, CVF w54); IEEE pp. 4037-4042, DOI 10.1109/CVPRW50498.2020.00475; arXiv 2004.02072 (Apr 2020)
rows.causality_evidence: The paper (Sec. 4) states its 'reported result in all the data sets is based on online decision making without seeing future video frames'. It criticises per-video normalisation. Features are pretrained YOLOv3 boxes/classes plus FlowNet2 optical-flow moments, followed by kNN distance and CUSUM. However, Sec. 3.2 describes frame labelling: after an alarm, frames from tau_start (last s_t=0) are relabelled anomalous, which is retroactive. tau_end is set after the statistic decreases for about 5 consecutive frames, which is look-ahead. In MOVAD (WACV 2022) and MTL (CVPRW 2022), the same authors explicitly call this start/end procedure 'offline localization'. The paper does not explain how a continuous AUC is obtained from this relabelling. No code is available to check score normalisation; the lab's MONAD code uses per-video min-max on Ped2. Per-video normalisation is therefore not proven for this paper, but the evaluation is not strictly causal.
rows.auc_table_ref: arXiv 2004.02072v1 Table 1 ('AuC result comparison on three datasets'). Fig. 2: any-shot curve on modified UCSD.
rows.fps_or_latency: Not reported for the full pipeline; it only says YOLO is fast.
rows.code_url: No code link in the paper. github.com/kevaldoshi17/Any-Shot-Anomaly-Detection exists but contains only LICENSE and a 28-byte README.
rows.notes: Table 1 for Ours is identical to the Continual Learning paper (86.4/97.8/71.62). Avenue 86.4 is also identical to MONAD and ODIT, although the motion features differ (FlowNet2 here vs GAN MSE there). Sultani et al. is listed at 71.5 on ShT.

rows.title: Continual Learning for Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Videos
rows.venue_year: CVPR 2020 Workshops (CVF w15); IEEE pp. 1025-1034, DOI 10.1109/CVPRW50498.2020.00135 (Crossref). The 'pp. 254-255' from survey citations does not match Crossref.
rows.causality_evidence: The pipeline is the same as Any-Shot (YOLOv3, FlowNet2 moments, kNN, CUSUM). Continual updates add human-labelled false-alarm vectors from tau_start to t. Sec. 4.5 says only that the ShanghaiTech result is 'based on online decision making without seeing future video frames'. It says per-video normalisation 'using the future frames' cannot be used online. The labelling rule (Sec. 3) relabels tau_start..tau_end after an alarm, which is retroactive plus about 5 frames of look-ahead. The authors later call this offline localization. Table 1 is described as general performance 'not necessarily with continual learning'. No code is available to check normalisation.
rows.auc_table_ref: CVF PDF Table 1 ('AuC result comparison on three datasets'). Fig. 5: continual-learning curve on modified UCSD.
rows.fps_or_latency: About 32 fps end-to-end (YOLOv3 about 83 fps, FlowNet2 about 40 fps) on an RTX 2070 with an i7-8700K. Continual update takes a few seconds (about 10 s of video).
rows.notes: The Table 1 results are numerically identical to Any-Shot. As with MONAD, the online claim is explicitly made only for ShT. Also tested qualitatively on an 8 h 23 min public CCTV YouTube stream.

rows.title: A Modular and Unified Framework for Detecting and Localizing Video Anomalies (MOVAD)
rows.causality_evidence: The paper itself separates the two: online detection is evaluated only with APD (precision vs normalised detection delay) on ShT. The frame-level AUC is in a table headed 'Offline Localization'. Localization rule: the detection instant marks the start. When the statistic drops for about 5 consecutive frames, the beginning of the drop window becomes the end. This needs future frames. Feature normalisation uses training min/max (causal). Online baselines (Liu, Morais, Luo) were re-run without per-video normalisation. The kNN-plus-CUSUM detection (simplified RNN) is causal, but no frame-AUC is presented as online.
rows.shtech_auc: 73.62 (offline localization); online APD 0.705 vs Liu 0.504, Morais 0.324, Luo 0.447
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 2 (offline localization AUC); Table 1 (online APD, ShT only); Table 3 (few-shot scene adaptation: Ped2 96.01, Avenue 80.68 at K=10); Table 4 (ShT per-module AUC: object detection 0.594, optical flow 0.703, pose 0.652). The CVF WACV PDF has the same numbers as arXiv v1.
rows.fps_or_latency: Not reported
rows.notes: Features: YOLOv4 (COCO), optical flow mean/variance in each box, and AlphaPose pose-prediction error. Whether the pose predictor is causal is not stated. The general RNN detector can be trained on synthetic kNN distances; the reported results use the fixed-weight CUSUM form. Without sequential detection, APD drops to 0.673.

rows.title: Multi-Task Learning for Video Surveillance with Limited Data
rows.venue_year: CVPR 2022 Workshops (CLVision), CVF pp. 3889-3899, DOI 10.1109/CVPRW56347.2022.00434
rows.causality_evidence: Sec. 4.1 says online detection is evaluated with APD and offline localization with frame-level AUC. Table 2 is titled 'Offline anomaly localization comparison in terms of frame-level AUC'. The paper argues that LSTM-based 'online' methods still normalise the statistic over a video segment. Motion features are normalised with training min/max. The frame AUC is not claimed to be causal, and the online metric (APD) covers ShT only.
rows.shtech_auc: 70.12 (offline localization); online APD 0.675
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 2 (offline localization AUC); Table 1 (APD on ShT); Tables 3-5 (cross-domain, trained on ShT camera 1).
rows.fps_or_latency: Not reported
rows.code_url: None (the paper links only the NVIDIA semantic-segmentation dependency)
rows.notes: Pipeline: SENet Faster R-CNN, FlowNet2, AlphaPose and HRNet-OCR segmentation produce labels, which are turned into Word2Vec semantic embeddings. A triplet-loss metric network is trained with generated 'pseudo-abnormal' semantic embeddings, hence the synthetic/pseudo-anomaly supervision label.

rows.title: Towards Interpretable Video Anomaly Detection
rows.causality_evidence: A sequential CUSUM-type detector monitors scene-graph interaction and pose statistics. Algorithm 1 is frame-by-frame, with a minimax detection-delay optimality claim. Sec. 4 lists 'online anomaly detection' among the things evaluated, but no online metric (APD or delay) is reported. The only Avenue/ShT AUC is in Table 4, titled 'Anomalous frame localization', which the authors' sibling papers treat as offline. The tau-hat backtracking (Eq. 9) is used for interpretation. The frame-labelling and normalisation protocol for the AUC is not described. This verdict is an inference: no causal evaluation is presented, and I found no direct proof of per-video normalisation.
rows.shtech_auc: 71.18 (Table 4); cross-domain trained on ShT cam 1: 0.689
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 4 (frame localization AUC); Table 3 (cross-domain overall); Table 2 (per-camera ShT AUC); Table 1 (interpretability Recall@5 0.373)
rows.fps_or_latency: Not reported
rows.notes: Components: YOLOv4, VGG-16 interaction model trained on VRD, AlphaPose with PoseFlow tracking, and Word2Vec. The metric MLP takes negatives from artificially generated anomalous interaction triplets. Confirmed: the 79.0/68.9 values seen in surveys are the cross-domain Table 3 numbers.

rows.title: Online Multivariate Anomaly Detection and Localization for High-Dimensional Settings (ODIT)
rows.venue_year: Sensors 22(21):8264, 2022, DOI 10.3390/s22218264 (Crossref); authors Mahsa Mozaffari, Keval Doshi, Yasin Yilmaz
rows.causality_evidence: Sec. 6.5: features are GAN future-frame-prediction MSE plus YOLOv3 box centre, area and class probabilities, fed to the ODIT kNN sequential statistic. The text says ODIT 'is based on online decision making and can detect anomalies in streaming videos in real-time'. It contrasts this with Liu et al.'s per-video normalisation. The same tau_start/tau_end relabelling is described, which is retroactive plus about 5 frames of look-ahead. The AUC numbers are exactly MONAD's. The only public code for this pipeline (the MONAD repo notebook, which prints 'ODIT AUC: 0.977' on Ped2) uses per-video min-max normalisation, per-test-video baselines, whole-video post-hoc pruning and a manually extrapolated ROC point.
rows.shtech_auc: 70.9 (107 test videos per text)
rows.auc_table_ref: Sensors 2022 Table 2 (Sec. 6.5, frame-level AUC, %)
rows.fps_or_latency: 25 fps end-to-end (limited by GAN feature extraction). The ODIT detector alone runs at over 40 fps with exact kNN and about 560 fps with approximate kNN on ShT.
rows.code_url: None in the paper (Data Availability: 'Not applicable'). The related notebook is at https://github.com/kevaldoshi17/Prediction-based-Video-Anomaly-Detection-
rows.notes: The video experiment is one application section of a general multivariate change-detection paper. It is effectively a re-report of the MONAD pipeline and numbers, not an independent result.

rows.title: Look at Adjacent Frames: Video Anomaly Detection without Offline Training
rows.causality_evidence: Sec. 3.1: a temporal DWT (Daubechies-2, n=16) runs over V_t, 'where the last frame of V_t is the current frame I_t'. Scoring starts at the 16th frame of each video. Eq. 10: the detection map for frame t is M_o^t, computed with the initial parameters theta_o^t before optimising on I_t. Those parameters come only from earlier frames via the adapter and clipper, so the frame-t score is causal (except t=0, which uses the post-optimisation map). Online here means test-time learning with no offline training (footnote 1). CANNOT REFUTE, BUT UNVERIFIED: the paper does not say how MSE is turned into the AUC score. Figs. 9 and 12 plot 'normalized MSE', so per-video min-max for the AUC cannot be ruled out. It is also not stated how the first 15 unscored frames of each video enter the AUC. No code is available.
rows.shtech_auc: 83.1 (79.8 without clipper). Evaluated on the 12 scenes that have test videos, which should be the standard test set, but the paper does not state the video count.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 1 (left: online baselines Giorno 2016 78.3 Avenue; Ionescu 2017 82.2/80.6; Liu 2018 87.5/84.4 on Ped2/Avenue, all reported on fewer videos); Table 2 (clipper ablation). arXiv v1 and v5 numbers are identical.
rows.fps_or_latency: Not reported. Each frame runs up to k=100 gradient-descent iterations (k=500 for the first 5 frames of each video), so it is likely far from real-time, but the paper gives no figure.
rows.code_url: None found (the author's GitHub account has 0 public repos)
rows.notes: Correction to the searcher: the model does NOT restart for every test video. Sec. 4 says that for non-continuous videos of the same scene, parameters are initialised from the last frame of the previous video stream. Only fully continuous single-camera streams start from random init. Test videos are therefore processed as a chained stream, which is still causal. Follow-up: Y. Ouyang's 2023 Warwick PhD thesis, 'Towards online solutions for detecting anomalous events in surveillance videos' (WRAP eprint 187376, 113 MB, not read).

rows.title: Strictly Causal Streaming Video Anomaly Detection with a Theoretically-Grounded State-Space Core
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2608.24810v1 (25 Aug 2026), single author Yogesh Kumar, cs.AI. No venue. The arXiv HTML rendering shows 'Journal: Pattern Recognition Letters', which comes from the LaTeX journal field, i.e. the intended target. The PDF does not contain it, and nothing shows the paper was accepted.
rows.causality_evidence: MODEL IS CAUSAL. Sec 3.4: the score at frame t is ||ê_t - e_t||, where ê_t is predicted from e_1..e_{t-1}. Sec 3.3.1 / Alg. 1: the update uses only s_{t-1} and x_t. EVALUATION IS NOT ONLINE. Sec 3.4 and Sec 5.1 say scores are 'min-max normalized per clip before thresholding/AUC computation', following [9] (Liu 2018). 'Clip' here means a whole test video (Ped2 has 12 test clips, Avenue 21). The released code confirms this (src/metrics.py frame_level_auc): it min-max normalises each clip, then concatenates all clips into one AUC. The detection-delay metric also uses the normalised scores. Neither the text nor the code applies temporal smoothing. Sec 5.5: no strict-causal vs windowed ablation was run, because a look-ahead variant was never implemented.
rows.ped2_auc: 67.9 (EER 36.8). Ablations: gate off 76.6; N=32 74.7; N=256 66.5; gate off + N=32 67.8
rows.avenue_auc: 70.2 (EER 34.9). Ablations: gate off 60.0; N=256 71.1; N=256 + slow decay 71.1
rows.shtech_auc: Not reported. Only 1 of 7 archive parts was obtained; the paper says results are 'left for a revision'. The repo has a ShanghaiTech config but no results.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 1 (main results); Table 3 (Ped2 ablations); Table 4 (Avenue ablations); Table 2 (theoretical vs measured delay)
rows.fps_or_latency: Table 1: 0.74 ms/frame, 1343.62 FPS (Ped2); 0.77 ms/frame, 1290.74 FPS (Avenue); Apple M3 Pro, PyTorch MPS. NEW FACT: the abstract calls this end-to-end latency, but src/evaluate.py (run_streaming_clip) times only model.step() on precomputed ResNet-18 embeddings. Features are cached, so the frozen backbone cost is NOT in the reported latency.
rows.notes: No baseline rows are rerun or reported under its own protocol. VADMamba is not reproduced (CUDA-only FlowNet2). Measured detection delay is 1.6 frames (Ped2) and 18.4 (Avenue), against a theoretical bound of 57 to 59. Backbone is a frozen ImageNet ResNet-18. Training uses normal-only data and causal 16-frame windows (40 epochs Ped2, 30 Avenue). The author calls the configuration untuned and well below SOTA. Not a strong rival on accuracy; the per-clip min-max means the reported AUC is not an online number.

rows.title: Spatiotemporal Anomaly Detection Using Deep Learning for Real-Time Video Surveillance (ISTL, incremental spatiotemporal learner)
rows.venue_year: IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics 16(1):393-402, 2020 (online 2019), DOI 10.1109/TII.2019.2938527. Authors confirmed via Semantic Scholar and dblp: Rashmika Nawaratne, Damminda Alahakoon, Daswin De Silva, Xinghuo Yu.
rows.causality_evidence: The paper exists, but I could NOT obtain the full text. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex mark it closed. The RMIT/figshare record (27527193) has no files. There is no arXiv version (arXiv author search for Nawaratne finds none). The abstract only says ISTL uses active learning with fuzzy aggregation to continuously update normality over time. That is an online-learning claim. The frame-scoring causality, per-video normalisation and smoothing could not be checked. 'not_found' here means the full text could not be found, not the paper.
rows.ped2_auc: Not verified from the primary source. Secondary: Pillai & Sen, GRSL 2022, Table I lists 'Nawaratne et al. [10]' at frame EER 8.9, AUC 91.1. Ata-Ur-Rehman, IEEE Access 2021, Table 2 lists 'Nawaratne et al [23]' Ped2 EER as 29.8, which conflicts.
rows.avenue_auc: Not verified. The 79.8 from the Sensors 2023 survey in the candidate summary was not checked by me.
rows.shtech_auc: Not verified; no secondary source I saw reports it.
rows.auc_table_ref: Primary unavailable. Secondary: Pillai & Sen GRSL 2022 Table I; Ata-Ur-Rehman IEEE Access 2021 Tables 1 to 3
rows.fps_or_latency: Secondary only: Ata-Ur-Rehman 2021 Tables 1 and 2 list 36.9 ms/frame (Ped1) and 38.1 ms/frame (Ped2) for Nawaratne [23]. Hardware unknown.
rows.notes: Secondary sources (and a search summary) say that new samples flagged by prediction error are confirmed by human feedback (active learning). If so, this is not a pure one-class or online-at-test protocol. It needs library or IEEE access to verify. The secondary EER figures disagree with each other (8.9 vs 29.8 on Ped2).

rows.title: Anomaly Detection With Particle Filtering for Online Video Surveillance
rows.venue_year: IEEE Access 9 (2021) 19457-19468, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2021.3054040 (open access, CC BY)
rows.causality_evidence: Read from the full PDF. It is a particle filter: the posterior p(z_t | z_{t-1}, w_t) is updated recursively per frame from a prediction model and a likelihood model over variable-size cells (Sec III). A frame is flagged if the estimated posterior falls below an empirically chosen threshold ε_o (Sec IV-C), and ROC curves come from sweeping that threshold. No per-video normalisation and no temporal smoothing are described. Causal by construction, as far as the text shows. BUT it does NOT meet the inclusion criterion: there is no frame-level AUC on Ped2, Avenue or ShanghaiTech.
rows.ped2_auc: No AUC reported. Ped2 frame EER is 29.5% (Table 2), with only an ROC curve (Fig. 8).
rows.shtech_auc: Not evaluated
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 1 (Ped1 EER 29%, 27 ms); Table 2 (Ped2 EER 29.5%, 25 ms); Table 3 (AUC on LIVE dataset only: 0.32)
rows.fps_or_latency: 25 ms/frame on Ped2 (about 40 FPS), 27 ms on Ped1, 27.3 ms on LIVE (Tables 1 to 3). Hardware not stated in the text.
rows.notes: Fails the AUC criterion; reports EER only on UCSD. The LIVE AUCs for every method in Table 3 are between 0.11 and 0.32 (below chance), and the Fig. 10 ROC curves sit near or below the diagonal. That looks suspicious, so treat the LIVE results with caution. The dictionary and clusters are built from training data. Not a usable AUC baseline.

rows.title: Anomaly detection in non-stationary videos using time-recursive differencing network based prediction
rows.venue_year: CORRECTION: IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters vol. 19, 2022, Art. no. 8010605, DOI 10.1109/LGRS.2021.3072191. The arXiv copy 2503.02234 was only posted on 4 Mar 2025. Authors: Gargi V. Pillai, Debashis Sen (IIT Kharagpur).
rows.causality_evidence: Sec II-B: block A_{m,n} is predicted from the same block in the previous p+d frames (time-recursive differencing plus ARMA, Eqs. 2 to 5). The paper says 'video frames are subjected to anomaly detection sequentially', and history blocks are restricted to non-anomalous ones. No score normalisation and no temporal smoothing are described. CAVEATS (could not refute, could not fully confirm): (1) active blocks must have foreground blocks 'in their immediate temporal neighborhood', and the paper does not say whether that includes frame n+1, so a 1-frame look-ahead is possible. (2) ARMA and AIC parameters are estimated from F=10 consecutive non-anomalous frames 'available before our prediction starts'; their source is not stated. (3) AUC depends strongly on the threshold λA (Table III: 74.0 at 0.001, 98.2 at 0.01, 94.1 at 0.1, 93.0 at 1). λA=0.01 was 'empirically determined', apparently on test results, and the paper does not explain how the ROC is traced from binary block decisions. Medium confidence.
rows.shtech_auc: Not evaluated
rows.auc_table_ref: Table I (Ped2 vs 20 methods); Table II (UMN AUC 99.7); Table III (sensitivity to λA, F, N)
rows.fps_or_latency: About 15 FPS on 240x360 frames, MATLAB, 3 GHz CPU, 16 GB RAM (Sec III-A). Uses KNN-matting segmentation and optical-flow magnitude.
rows.code_url: The paper cites github.com/gvp12/videoanomaly-detection, which returns 404 (probably a line-break hyphen lost in the PDF). The real repo, github.com/gvp12/video-anomaly-detection (pushed Feb 2021), contains only a README and example images, no code.
rows.notes: There is no weight training on the training split. The model is fitted per block from a few assumed-normal frames, so 'training_free' is approximate. Evaluated on Ped2, UMN and aerial datasets only. Speed is low and the AUC is tuned to the threshold. Treat 98.2 with caution. The related IEEE TAI 2024 paper by the same authors was not verified.

rows.title: Sequential Keypoint Density Estimator: an Overlooked Baseline of Skeleton-Based Video Anomaly Detection (SeeKer)
rows.venue_year: ICCV 2025 (Highlight); arXiv 2506.18368 (v1 23 Jun 2025, v3 3 Sep 2025). Authors: Anja Delić, Matej Grcić, Siniša Šegvić.
rows.causality_evidence: MODEL IS CAUSAL. It models p(X_t | X_<t) with masked causal layers over a sliding window of T preceding frames (Sec 3, Sec 4). EVALUATION IS NOT CAUSAL. Sec 4: (a) the first T-1 frames get the score of frame T, which is look-ahead; (b) Gaussian smoothing with σ=10 is applied per person, then the max is taken over persons. Code check (github adelic99/seeker): utils/scoring_utils.py and validation.py use scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter1d, a symmetric centred kernel, applied repeatedly per person, and validation.py smooths the per-frame clip scores again (smooth_scores(scores_arr, 2)). AUROC is micro, over concatenated frames. I saw no per-video min-max. Table 7 removes the smoothing but keeps the backtracking.
rows.avenue_auc: Not evaluated. Sec 4 skips Avenue (and UCF-Crime) because pose extraction and tracking work poorly on it.
rows.shtech_auc: 85.5 full test set / 86.9 human-related subset, with smoothing (Table 2). Without smoothing: 83.4 / 84.9 (Table 7; values match the candidate's reading). For comparison, STG-NF without smoothing is 83.0 / 84.4.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 2 (ShanghaiTech); Table 7 (smoothing ablation); Table 1 (UBnormal)
rows.fps_or_latency: No FPS or latency reported. It only claims real-time feasibility. Training uses 0.76 GB GPU memory and takes under 10 min on an RTX 3090 (App. C.4).
rows.notes: Skeleton-only, so it misses non-human anomalies. Hyperparameters are validated on UBnormal val and reused for ShanghaiTech. Skeletons and tracks come from an upstream pose and tracking pipeline; I did not check whether that tracker is causal. The no-smoothing 83.4 is the closest to an online number, but it still includes the frame-T backtracking.

rows.title: Local Anomaly Detection in Videos using Object-Centric Adversarial Learning (GARDiN-VAD)
rows.venue_year: ICPR 2020 Workshops (1st Int. Workshop on Deep Learning for Human-Centric Activity Understanding); arXiv 2011.06722 (13 Nov 2020). Authors: Pankaj Raj Roy, Guillaume-Alexandre Bilodeau, Lama Seoud.
rows.causality_evidence: MODEL IS CAUSAL. It uses the current object appearance and a past spatial-gradient image from T=3 frames earlier (Sec 3.1). Sec 2 says it 'only relies on the previous frame for gradient', making it real-time applicable, and Sec 4.3 says it relies 'only on the past and present observations'. EVALUATION IS NOT ONLINE. Sec 3.4 normalises scores between 0 and 1 'for each sequence independently', following the protocol of [10] (Liu 2018). Sec 3.5 applies a Gaussian filter with std 10 'throughout the sequence', which is centred and non-causal. Sec 4.2 computes AUC on the concatenated scores of all videos.
rows.shtech_auc: 81.1 (CenterNet); 80.3 (RetinaNet)
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 1 (also Ped1 85.2, UMN 99.7); Table 3 (detector comparison); Table 2 (Ped2 ablations)
rows.fps_or_latency: About 80 ms/frame, i.e. 12.5 FPS: about 75 ms for object detection and gradient extraction plus about 5 ms for GARDiN and ALREC-FL, assuming about 5 objects per frame. Intel i5-9400F, RTX 2070 (Sec 4.5).
rows.code_url: none found (the paper gives no repository)
rows.notes: Training videos are assumed normal. The second stage trains a discriminator against GAN-generated samples, but no real anomalies are used. The reported AUCs need the per-video min-max plus centred σ=10 smoothing, so they are not comparable to an online protocol.

rows.title: Predicting Next Local Appearance for Video Anomaly Detection (NLAPnet)
rows.venue_year: MVA 2021 (oral); arXiv 2106.06059 (10 Jun 2021). Authors: Pankaj Raj Roy, Guillaume-Alexandre Bilodeau, Lama Seoud.
rows.causality_evidence: G predicts a_i^{t+T} from (a_i^{t-T}, a_i^t), with T=3. NEW FACT: Sec 2.3 produces the region score s_i^t at time t from the triplet <a^{t-T}, a^t, a^{t+T}>, and crops are taken at t-T, t and t+T using frame t's box (Sec 2.1). So the score assigned to frame t uses frame t+3, a 3-frame look-ahead in label alignment. Sec 2.3 smooths frame scores temporally with a Gaussian filter, and evaluation follows the protocol of [5] (Liu et al. FFP). The code (proy3/NLAP-net_VAD, src/utilities.py get_results, defaults in src/defines.py) applies min-max normalisation (DEFAULT_NORMALIZE_SCORES=True) over each scores_data, which appears to hold one sequence, and then scipy gaussian_filter1d with DEFAULT_SMOOTHING_FACTOR=10, which is centred.
rows.ped2_auc: NLAPnet-hg 97.2; NLAPnet-dla 96.3. Few-shot fine-tune from ShanghaiTech: 96.5/96.8/97.5 for 1/5/10 shots.
rows.shtech_auc: NLAPnet-hg 82.5; NLAPnet-dla 82.0
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 1 (also Ped1 82.3 hg / 81.1 dla); Table 2 (few-shot scene adaptation); Table 3 (ShanghaiTech ablation, full model 82.2)
rows.fps_or_latency: Table 4 (ShanghaiTech): inference 34 FPS (NLAPnet-dla), 13 FPS (NLAPnet-hg). Intel i7-8700, RTX 2080, Keras/TensorFlow.
rows.notes: Object-centric, using a CenterNet detector pretrained on COCO. Real-time only with the DLA backbone. All reported AUCs combine the t+3 look-ahead, per-video min-max and centred σ=10 smoothing, so they are not online numbers.

rows.title: Cerberus: Real-Time Video Anomaly Detection via Cascaded Vision-Language Models
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2510.16290v1 (18 Oct 2025). No venue. The PDF still carries the ACM template placeholder 'Conference'17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA' and leftover Chinese author notes around Figs. 10 and 11 (a draft). Authors: Yue Zheng, Xiufang Shi, Jiming Chen, Yuanchao Shu.
rows.causality_evidence: Verdict is conservative: I found no explicit look-ahead, but the paper never shows causality. Online stage: motion ratio p(D_t) from |F_t - F_{t-1}| (Eq. 4, causal); a CLIP 'health score' per 'segment s' over the top-k rules and perturbed labels (Eq. 5, Alg. 1); then Qwen2.5-VL captioning and Qwen3-Embedding classification. Segment length and formation are never defined. The paper never says what score frames dropped by the motion filter get, and describes no smoothing or normalisation. The motion and prompt thresholds ε and α were chosen on a ShanghaiTech subset (Fig. 11, 91.93 AUC). The rule-evolution experiments feed back user labels from one half of each test set. The Table 8 ablation uses a 10% frame sample of ShanghaiTech. No code is available to check.
rows.avenue_auc: 86.40 absolute (Table 7, Cerberus Base); +2.28 with a customised rule. Relative to AnomalyRuler: 96.87% (Table 5).
rows.shtech_auc: 82.73 absolute (Tables 6, 7 and 9); +1.82 customised in Table 7, although the text says 3.82. Relative 98.13% (Table 5). Table 8 reports the same 82.73 on a 10% frame subset, so it is unclear whether the headline figure covers the full 107-video test set.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 5 (relative AUC and fps); Table 7 (absolute Avenue/SHTech); Table 9 (SHTech 82.73, Campus 73.75); Table 8 (ShanghaiTech subset ablation)
rows.fps_or_latency: On the ORIGINAL test sets: 4.76 fps (Avenue) and 4.90 fps (ShanghaiTech), 4.74 fps on average (Tables 5 and 7). The headline 57.68 fps is reached only on test sets diluted to 1% anomalies by duplicating normal frames (23.96 fps at 5%). NVIDIA L40S, Xeon 8352V.
rows.notes: The real-time claim does not hold on the standard benchmarks (about 4.8 fps). Absolute AUCs appear only in ablation and customisation tables. Rules are induced offline from normal frames using Qwen2.5-VL-7B and DeepSeek-R1, with no weight training. UCF-Crime and XD-Violence are excluded. Weak evidence; not a verified online competitor.

rows.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Video Anomaly Detection in the Wild: Online Learning and Inference for Real-world Deployment
rows.venue_year: CVPR 2024 Workshops (ABAW), CVF open access (pp. 4832-4841 and DOI 10.1109/CVPRW63382.2024.00486 come from search-result metadata only, not checked); arXiv 2404.18747 (29 Apr 2024)
rows.causality_evidence: 'Online' here means online LEARNING: weights are updated on streaming CHAD data ('a lag of two time steps'). The ShanghaiTech AUCs (Table 2, 'Evaluation of Models Pre-trained on Shanghaitech') are offline-trained TSGAD, GEPC and STG-NF evaluated offline. The windows are 30 frames (TSGAD, GEPC) and 24 frames (STG-NF) with stride 1. Neither the arXiv nor the CVPRW text says whether a window ends at frame t, which frame receives the window score, or whether smoothing or normalisation is applied. If STG-NF's official scoring was reused (the paper does not say), it is non-causal: utils/scoring_utils.py assigns each window's score to frame start + seg_len/2 (the centre), and smooth_scores() applies gaussian_filter1d per test video with sigma 1..6 cumulatively (centred).
rows.shtech_auc: Offline-pretrained models only: TSGAD 0.742, GEPC 0.729, STG-NF 0.851 (AUC-ROC; AUC-PR 0.602 / 0.614 / 0.869). None of these is an online-inference result.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 2 (same values in arXiv v1 and the CVPRW PDF)
rows.fps_or_latency: not reported (it only says the windows match 'the standard frame rate of surveillance cameras')
rows.code_url: None given in the paper. A related paper from the same group points to github.com/TeCSAR-UNCC/TSGAD (search result, not verified).
rows.notes: Confirmed near-miss. The online adaptation results are on CHAD only. Retention is 89.39% in the abstract and 89.38% in the conclusion. It does not qualify as an online ShanghaiTech, Avenue or Ped2 competitor.

rows.title: Rethinking Video Anomaly Detection - A Continual Learning Approach
rows.venue_year: WACV 2022, pp. 3961-3970 in the CVF open-access version (no arXiv version found); IEEE Xplore pp. 3036-3045, DOI 10.1109/WACV51458.2022.00309 (Crossref record checked 2026-11-06: title, authors Doshi and Yilmaz, container 2022 IEEE/CVF WACV, page 3036-3045)
rows.causality_evidence: Design-level only. The intro says anomalous activity detection 'must be online'. The decision is a single-hidden-layer LSTM 'with a two input time steps' over kNN distances to the nominal feature set. The paper does not say explicitly that the two steps are t-1 and t. Features are 'normalized to [0, 1] using the maximum and minimum values from training', so there is no test-video normalisation, and no score smoothing is described. The paper says frame-level AUC 'is only suitable for anomalous frame localization', which 'can be offline'. It proposes Average Precision Delay (APD), the area under precision vs normalised average detection delay. Causality is not verifiable from code because none is released. Direct CVF fetches returned 403, so the PDF text was read through the r.jina.ai reader. One attempt to open the CVF PDF in the built-in browser pane triggered a file-download/save dialog on the user's screen. I did not complete or retry it.

rows.title: Real-Time Video Anomaly Detection Using YOLO Pose Estimation and CLIP-Based Semantic Scoring
rows.venue_year: IEEE MIPR 2026 (9th; arXiv comment says accepted for IEEE Xplore); arXiv 2608.31074 (31 Aug 2026)
rows.causality_evidence: The paper never uses 'online', 'causal' or 'streaming'; it claims only real-time throughput. Sec. III-C quote: 'Raw scores are smoothed with a one-dimensional Gaussian kernel (σ=5, half-window w=15) to suppress transient fluctuations.' The paper does not say whether the kernel is centred or one-sided. A 'half-window' of 15 = 3σ matches a standard symmetric (centred) kernel, which would need 15 future frames, but this is an inference. The paper also does not say whether AUROC uses raw or smoothed scores. The threshold θ=0.7 is chosen 'by sweeping [0.1,0.9] on a validation partition to maximize the AUROC', which is odd because AUROC is threshold-free. No per-video min-max normalisation is mentioned.
rows.shtech_auc: 70.26 (the test split is not stated: the paper cites only totals of 437 videos and 317,398 frames, never the 107-video test set)
rows.auc_table_ref: Table I (frame-level AUROC %, 'Proposed' row)
rows.fps_or_latency: 51.39 FPS end-to-end on an NVIDIA Titan XP vs 15.32 for the baseline (Table III). Components: YOLO v11n-pose 87.76 FPS, CLIP scoring 124.04 FPS. Live deployment: about 10 FPS per feed over 5 CCTV feeds. No ms latency given.
rows.notes: Supervision caveats: CLIP ViT-B/32 scoring is zero-shot with fixed prompts. The YOLO detector, however, is fine-tuned on 2,864 augmented images from 1,154 labelled CU Indoor frames, and the threshold is tuned on a validation partition. Red flag: the Avenue and ShanghaiTech values are IDENTICAL to the multi-feature density-estimation baseline (89.26 / 70.26), with footnote ‡ saying it 'Shares the same YOLO detector and evaluation as †; only the scoring stage differs'. Only CU Indoor differs (84.13 vs 82.12). This counterexample is confirmed: real-time is not the same as online.

rows.title: Video Anomaly Detection with Structured Keywords (VADSK)
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2503.10653 (7 Mar 2025), no venue listed; single author Thomas Foltz
rows.causality_evidence: Each frame gets its own VLM description, which is converted to a keyword encoding and passed to an NN classifier. Abstract: 'These results are achieved without temporal context'. No temporal smoothing and no score normalisation are described (the only L2 normalisation is on the keyword-weight vector). Per-frame scoring is causal by construction. The evaluation protocol, however, is non-standard and supervised (see notes).
rows.shtech_auc: 0.753 in Tables 1 and 2 (abstract says 0.745; Sec. 4.4 text says 74.2). NON-STANDARD protocol.
rows.auc_table_ref: Table 2 (frame-level AUROC comparison); Table 1 (ablation: Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct 0.865 / 0.753 / 0.742; MiniCPM-V-2.6-int4 0.865 / 0.707 / 0.604)
rows.fps_or_latency: Not real time in practice: 5.17-5.77 s per frame with Llama-3.2-11B-Vision (4-bit) and 2.09-2.43 s per frame with MiniCPM (Table 1). Hardware not stated.
rows.notes: NOT COMPARABLE. 'Our work only uses the test dataset due to our supervised binary classification approach.' Also: 'We used 80% of the frames for training and 20% for testing', with 5-fold cross-validation and a weighted BCE classifier trained on anomalous labels. A random frame-level split also leaks temporally adjacent frames between train and test. Table 2 lists 'Towards Interpretable VAD' as ShT 0.689 / Avenue 0.790, which are Doshi WACV 2023's cross-domain numbers, not in-domain ones.

(97.2 / 73.62 / 88.7), Ouyang [53] ECCVW 2022 'Look at adjacent frames' (96.5 / 83.1 / 90.2), Li [71] ST-CAAE TMM 2020 (Ped2 87.1). rows.title: VigilFormer: Deformable Attention for Video Anomaly Detection with Causal Risk Inference
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2606.14724 (31 May 2026), no venue; single author Xinze Zhang
rows.causality_evidence: Causality is claimed ONLY for the classifier head (CAC, dilated causal convolutions): 'Causal convolutions ensure that the prediction at time t depends only on current and past features', 'which matches the online inference setting'. Four things go against an online evaluation. (1) Sec. 3.5: 'At inference, features are extracted for the full video'. (2) The DSTE deformable attention predicts unconstrained sampling offsets over 'the feature sequence', and nothing says it is masked to past positions. (3) Features come from non-overlapping 16-frame I3D clips with 10-crop features pre-extracted, which gives up to 15 frames of look-ahead within a snippet. (4) The snippet-to-frame mapping used for frame AUC is never described. No smoothing or normalisation of scores is described; the EMA in Eq. 8 drives frame skipping only.
rows.avenue_auc: 89.74 (weakly supervised protocol; the paper does not explain how video-level labels were applied to Avenue)
rows.shtech_auc: 97.21 (weak-supervision setting, but the paper states 'Following the standard protocol, 330 videos are used for training and 107 for testing'. The 330 one-class training videos are all normal, so MIL as described cannot be run on that split. Not comparable to the one-class campus protocol.)

Other quality red flags: (1) unsupervised STG-NF appears in the weak tables at 85.90 (UCF-Crime) and 96.75 (ShT); 85.9 appears to be STG-NF's own published one-class ShanghaiTech AUC (from memory, not re-checked). (2) The text claims +3.83 over RTFM while the table gives 3.80. (3) Sec. 2.2 describes 3-D offsets while Sec. 3 uses a 1-D sequence.

rows.title: MoniTor: Exploiting Large Language Models with Instruction for Online Video Anomaly Detection
rows.causality_evidence: Appendix B: 'online VAD aims to detect anomalies in streaming videos with minimal processing delay, without accessing future frames.' Sec. 4.1: 'ensuring no future information leakage'. Memory uses past frames only (long-term memory: previous 10 frame summaries; short-term: 2 most recent frames; caption cleaning: current plus previous 5). The score weighting blends the current score with the previous score, which is causal. No smoothing or normalisation is described. The interval-score-to-frame mapping used for AUC is not described.

rows.auc_table_ref: UCF-Crime (Tables 1, 4-7) and XD-Violence (Table 2) only

rows.title: Online anomaly detection in surveillance videos with asymptotic bound on false alarm rate (MONAD) [EXTRA row: listed as already known; new facts found]
rows.venue_year: Pattern Recognition 114 (2021) 107865; arXiv 2010.07110 v1 (10 Oct 2020), titled '...with Asymptotic Bounds on False Alarm Rate'
rows.causality_evidence: PAPER (arXiv v1): the method is causal by design. Frame t is predicted from {X1..Xt-1} (window 4). The instantaneous kNN evidence δt feeds a CUSUM s_t = max{s_{t-1}+δt, 0} (Eq. 8). Sec. 4.5 states the 'reported result in the ShanghaiTech dataset is based on online decision making without seeing future video frames' and criticises per-video normalisation. The no-look-ahead claim covers ShanghaiTech only, not Avenue or Ped2. After an alarm, frames between τstart and τend are relabelled, where τend requires 5 consecutive decreasing frames (post-hoc). RELEASED CODE (MONAD.ipynb, Ped2 only) refutes causality for Ped2 in four ways. (1) The AUC is computed on AV2.append((vid-np.min(vid))/(np.max(vid)-np.min(vid))), i.e. per-test-video min-max normalisation. (2) Per-video baselines are hard-coded, lm2 = [0.75,...,0.95,0.85,...], with the comment 'computed per video by using the base lm and computing the mean and variance for each video'. (3) Scores are zeroed with look-ahead over the positive indices (idx[id1+6], idx[id2+50]). (4) 'fpr2 = np.sort(np.append(fpr2,(0.45)))' with tpr 1 adds an extrapolated ROC point before metrics.auc. The printed result is 'ODIT AUC: 0.977'.
rows.ped2_auc: 97.2 (paper Table 1). The released notebook prints 0.977 with the non-causal procedure above.
rows.avenue_auc: 86.4 (paper Table 1; the Sensors survey omits this value)
rows.shtech_auc: 70.9 (paper Table 1; claimed online with no per-video normalisation, but there is no ShT code to verify it)
rows.auc_table_ref: arXiv v1 Table 1 'AuROC result comparison on three datasets' (journal-version tables not checked)
rows.fps_or_latency: GAN frame predictor about 22 fps; YOLOv3 12 ms (about 83 fps); RTX 2070 with an i7-8700K. No combined end-to-end figure.
rows.notes: The most important new fact: the paper's ShanghaiTech 70.9 is explicitly claimed as a causal evaluation, but the only public evaluation code (Ped2) uses per-video normalisation, test-video statistics, look-ahead pruning and an extrapolated ROC point. Treat the Ped2 and Avenue numbers as non-causal or unverified. The notebook labels the result 'ODIT AUC', so it may not match the paper's exact run (0.977 vs 97.2). The arXiv comments note overlap with arXiv 2004.07941 (CVPRW 2020).

rows.title: Towards Interpretable Video Anomaly Detection [EXTRA row: found while verifying the survey's Doshi 2023 entry]
rows.venue_year: WACV 2023, pp. 2655-2664 (Keval Doshi, Yasin Yilmaz)
rows.causality_evidence: Design-level only. Algorithm 1 runs 'while st < h: t←t+1; Get video frame Ft ... Calculate δt and st'. Here δt = log d_t² − log d_α² (kNN distance to the nominal set) and st = max{st−1+δt, 0} (CUSUM, Eq. 6). Not stated: whether the pose branch's 'fixed length segments from a person's trajectory' end at t, which score feeds the frame AUC, and whether any per-video normalisation is applied. No code was found. Given that the same group's PR-2021 code normalises per video, treat this as unverified at evaluation level.

Supervision is mixed: the interaction detector is trained on the external VRD dataset, the interaction-monitoring MLP is trained with 'artificial anomalous interactions', and the pose branch is trained on nominal data. This paper shows that the survey's and VADSK's 68.9/79.0 figures are cross-domain numbers.

rows.title: STEP: Score-Based Temporal Energy for Human Pose Video Anomaly Detection
rows.venue_year: ECCV 2026 (accepted per arXiv comments); arXiv 2608.19987 v1, 20 Aug 2026
rows.causality_evidence: CONFIRMED ONLY for the appendix 'Online Raw' protocol, not for the headline numbers. Sec 4.1: each sequence is scored from the current frame plus the preceding T-1 frames (T=12). AUROC is micro-averaged 'without any video-level normalization', but the main protocol applies 'temporal Gaussian 1D-smoothing' (refs SeeKer, STG-NF, MULDE), so Table 1 (ShT 86.2) is smoothed. In the code this is scipy gaussian_filter1d per clip, which is centred (non-causal); the ShanghaiTech default frame sigma is 13. App. C.6: Backtrack (SeeKer) is described as offline and non-causal. Online scores the preceding T frames and assigns the score to 'the current frame t or the center (T/2)', and the paper calls Online Raw 'the only true zero-delay protocol'. The released code (evaluation/evaluator.py) implements both variants: Online_Latest puts the score on the last frame of the window (causal), and Online_Center, labelled 'STG-NF', puts it on start+T/2, which is about 6 frames of look-ahead. The paper does not say which variant Table S7's 'On' columns use. Pose normalisation is per window, using that window's own mean and std of y (causal). Energies are z-scored per noise scale with training-set statistics (causal). Frames without a person are filled with the global min minus 1, a constant at the bottom of the ranking (harmless). EXTRA CAVEAT from train.py: 'ShanghaiTech has no validation split (test aliased to validate)', and the best checkpoint is selected by smoothed Online_Latest AUC on the ShT TEST set. It is unclear whether the paper's mean-over-20-runs numbers use best_model or final_model.
rows.avenue_auc: not reported (the code has an Avenue loader but the paper reports no results)
rows.shtech_auc: Causal: Online Raw (Agg-Max, Full) 83.55 AUC / 81.41 AP; Human-Related split 85.12. Non-causal: Table 1 headline 86.2 +/- 0.1 (Full) and 87.7 +/- 0.1 (HR), both smoothed. Other Table S7 values: On+Smooth 86.32, BT Raw 83.93, BT+Smooth 85.39. Uses the standard 107-video test set (Sec 4.1: '330 training and 107 test videos').
rows.auc_table_ref: Main Table 1 (smoothed, mean of 20 runs). Appendix C.6 Table S7 (BT/On x Raw/Smooth, single configuration).
rows.fps_or_latency: Sec 4.4 and Table S10, GTX 1080, scoring only, pose extraction excluded (K=48, T=12): 0.86 ms (1167 FPS) at 1 person/frame, 0.97 ms (1026 FPS) at 50 persons, 1.62 ms (618 FPS) at 100 persons. Poses come from the precomputed AlphaPose output of STG-NF.
rows.notes: Pose-based (skeleton), so it needs a pose detector and tracker; the tracker's causality was not checked. UBnormal Online Raw 85.03 (Full). For a fair online comparison, use 83.55 (ShT On Raw), not 86.2. Main-paper Table 1 also lists STG-NF 85.9 and SeeKer 85.5, which are smoothed/non-causal baselines.

rows.title: VADSK: Video Anomaly Detection with Structured Keywords
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2503.10653 v1, 7 Mar 2025 (preprint; single author Thomas Foltz, Penn State)
rows.causality_evidence: Scoring is causal per frame: VLM caption, then a keyword encoding, then an MLP, with no temporal context and no smoothing or normalisation (Sec 3.2, Sec 4.6: 'we do not require temporal information'). BUT the evaluation protocol is not one-class and is not comparable. The induction step uses 'random frames known to be anomalies from the test set' (Sec 3.1.1). Code src/deduct.py filters labels.csv to TEST-split frames only, applies train_test_split(test_size=0.2) as a random frame-level split, and trains a BCE classifier on 80% of the labelled test frames, including anomalies. ROC-AUC is then computed on the remaining random 20% of frames.

rows.title: Follow the Rules: Reasoning for Video Anomaly Detection with Large Language Models (AnomalyRuler)
rows.causality_evidence: CONFIRMED non-causal (Sec 4.1, Perception Smoothing). Step I is a causal EMA, s_t. Step II is a majority vote 'within a window centered at each EMA value s_i with a padding size p', summing over j from max(1,i-p) to min(i+p,t), with p=5 by default (Sec 5.1). That is 5 frames of look-ahead. The vote threshold tau is 'the mean of all EMA values', tau = (1/t)*sum of s_i over the whole video, which is per-video information. The final anomaly score a_t is a second EMA over these smoothed labels, so the non-causality carries into the AUC.

rows.title: Efficient Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection via Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF)
rows.venue_year: WACV 2027 (accepted per arXiv comments); arXiv 2610.32486 v1, 23 Oct 2026
rows.causality_evidence: CONFIRMED non-causal in two places. (1) Sec 3.3.1, Eq 20: video-level fusion uses a clip C_t = {f_(t-k), ..., f_t, ..., f_(t+k)}. Sec 4.1 calls it 'a temporal clip of 10 frames centered at the anchor', which is look-ahead. (2) Sec 4.1: 'apply Gaussian smoothing with sigma=100' on the dense per-frame score sequence, about 3.3 s at 30 fps, following Unified-reasoning. The causal parts are EMA thresholds with a statistic freeze (Eqs 9-13), a drift anchor over the preceding W=20 frames (Eq 6), and forward-only score propagation (Eq 24, M=64). The Stage-2 result without smoothing (frame-level anchor scores propagated forward, no centred clip) looks causal, but the paper does not present it as an online protocol.
rows.shtech_auc: 80.54 +/- 0.03 (full pipeline, non-causal). Stage 2 only, no smoothing: 71.38 (apparently causal; my reading, not a stated protocol). Stage 2 + smoothing: 77.19. Stage 3 without refinement: 75.50. The ShT dataset is cited as Luo et al. 2017 [17]. Table 3 lists 2,550 stride-16 candidates, about 40.8k frames, which matches the 107-video test set (my inference).

rows.title: Online Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Videos with Asymptotic Bounds on False Alarm Rate (MONAD)
rows.venue_year: Pattern Recognition 114 (2021) 107865; arXiv 2010.07110 (Oct 2020)
rows.causality_evidence: NEW FACTS. The method itself is causal: a GAN predicts the next frame from the past 4 frames, YOLOv3 features feed a kNN distance to normal training features, and a CUSUM statistic s_t = max(s_(t-1) + delta_t, 0) is updated (Eqs 7-8). The paper says 'our reported result in the ShanghaiTech dataset is based on online decision making without seeing future video frames' and criticises per-video normalisation. The online claim is stated explicitly only for ShT. After an alarm, frames are relabelled back to tau_start, which is retroactive. REFUTATION from the released code (MONAD.ipynb, the Ped2 path): (a) lm2 is a per-video baseline list, with the comment 'computed per video by using the base lm and computing the mean and variance for each video'; (b) a post-hoc pass over the whole video's positive-index list zeroes scores using future indices, e.g. idx[id1+6]-idx[id1]>=10; (c) per-video min-max normalisation (vid-min(vid))/(max(vid)-min(vid)) is applied before the AUC; (d) the ROC is padded with an extrapolated point (FPR 0.45, TPR 1) 'so as to complete the ROC curve'. So at least the released Ped2 evaluation is non-causal and inflated. The ShT and Avenue evaluation code is not released.

rows.title: Strictly Causal Streaming Video Anomaly Detection with a Theoretically-Grounded State-Space Core
rows.venue_year: arXiv 2608.24810 v1, 25 Aug 2026 (preprint; header lists the journal Pattern Recognition Letters, probably a submission)
rows.causality_evidence: NEW FACTS confirm the known caveat. Eq 7: the score s_t = ||e_hat_t - e_t||_2 uses the prediction made one step earlier, from e_1 to e_(t-1), so the model is strictly causal. However, the paper also states that 'scores are min-max normalized per clip before thresholding/AUC computation' (Sec 3), and Sec 5 says it uses 'the standard per-clip min-max score normalization protocol [7]'. The reported AUCs therefore use per-video information.
